attackPath.dataflow: Source: OkHttp TLS handshake to platform 443 (AG-UI SSE, upload, login-adjacent calls). Transform: WhitelistTrustManager.checkServerTrusted returns immediately when socket/engine peer IP is in TRUSTED_HOSTS; hostnameVerifier returns true for whitelisted host strings. Sink: OkHttp session established with attacker-supplied certificate; Bearer token, chat/TTS content, and uploaded bytes flow through the attacker.
attackPath.reachability: Attacker on the same LAN segment (ARP spoofing 10.0.18.166) receives the connection because OkHttp is pinned to Proxy.NO_PROXY; the socket peer address still reads 10.0.18.166, so the whitelist matches and any self-signed attacker certificate is accepted with no prompt or pin check.

confidence.rationale: Bypass conditions are unconditional in code and the full source-to-sink chain was traced line-by-line.

findings.remediation: Replace the early-return in WhitelistTrustManager.checkServerTrusted with pinning: bundle the expected self-signed certificate (or its SPKI SHA-256) for each whitelisted IP and compare the leaf certificate before accepting; keep the default TrustManager for all other hosts and remove the hostnameVerifier bypass (verify the expected IP/CN mapping instead). Add a unit test asserting a mismatched certificate for 10.0.18.166 fails the handshake.
remediationTests: Handshake against a MockWebServer presenting an unrelated self-signed certificate while the client targets a whitelisted host must fail.
findings.rootCause: The convenience feature 'trust self-signed certs for intranet hosts' was implemented as 'skip all validation for whitelisted IPs' instead of pinning the expected certificate, collapsing both certificate-chain validation and hostname verification to no-ops for the primary server channel.
findings.summary: The custom X509ExtendedTrustManager accepts any certificate for the three whitelisted intranet IPs and the hostname verifier is bypassed for them, so an on-path LAN attacker can impersonate the platform 443 endpoint, intercept bearer tokens and uploaded files, and inject SSE/TTS content.
findings.title: TLS certificate validation bypassed for whitelisted intranet hosts

validation.counterevidence: Endpoints are fixed intranet IPs and the deployment is documented as intranet-only; this bounds exposure to LAN-adjacent attackers but does not defeat the finding because the threat model explicitly includes on-path LAN attackers.
validation.evidence: HttpClients.kt:79 and 85 return before delegate.checkServerTrusted for whitelisted peer addresses; lines 47-49 hostnameVerifier short-circuits to true for TRUSTED_HOSTS; the shared client carries Authorization: Bearer headers (AguiClient.kt:742, AguiClient.kt:665) over this channel.
validation.method: Static source-to-sink trace of the full OkHttp TLS configuration in HttpClients.create() and every consumer of HttpClients.shared.

attackPath.dataflow: Source: NetConfig.DEFAULT_PLATFORM_BASE = http://10.0.18.166:8080. Transform: NetEndpoints.loginUrl appends /login without scheme upgrade; AguiClient.login builds {username,password} JSON and POSTs via the shared cleartext-permitted OkHttp client. Sink: credentials transmitted in plaintext on every login and every ~25-minute token refresh.
attackPath.reachability: Any passive observer on the device LAN segment (managed-switch mirror port, rogue AP, ARP-spoofed host) captures the POST body directly; no TLS downgrade is needed because the connection is cleartext end to end.

confidence.rationale: Default constant, cleartext allowlist, and the exact POST body are directly verified in source; behavior is deterministic.

findings.remediation: Serve login over the existing 443 reverse proxy (e.g. POST https://{host}/ai-server/auth/login) and switch NetEndpoints.loginUrl to derive the https:// URL from the platform host exactly as agentStreamUrl already does; if :8080 must remain for legacy devices, gate cleartext login behind an explicit settings opt-in and stop re-sending the password by extending token refresh.
remediationTests: Contract test asserting loginUrl() starts with https:// whenever platformBase host is set.
findings.rootCause: Only the agent-stream endpoint was migrated behind the 443 self-signed reverse proxy; the login endpoint kept the original intranet HTTP :8080 contract, so the most sensitive request in the app is the only one that never upgrades to TLS.
findings.summary: The platform account and password are POSTed as JSON over cleartext HTTP by default (http://10.0.18.166:8080), and the ~25-minute token expiry re-sends the password on every re-login, letting a passive on-path attacker harvest the admin credentials.
findings.title: Platform login sends account and password over cleartext HTTP

validation.counterevidence: Deployment docs treat 10.0.18.166 as intranet-only and the platform may not offer TLS on :8080 at all (server-side constraint outside this repository); this bounds impact to the intranet threat model rather than eliminating it.
validation.evidence: NetConfig.kt:90 default base is http://; network_security_config.xml:7-11 explicitly permits cleartext to 10.0.18.166; AguiClient.kt:283-296 sends the credential body on every fresh login; TokenPolicy.TTL_MS = 25min forces periodic re-login.
validation.method: Static trace of the login flow from NetConfig defaults through NetEndpoints.loginUrl to the OkHttp POST, cross-checked against network_security_config.xml.

attackPath.dataflow: Source: user-entered account/password/API keys plus the platform bearer token after login. Transform: NetConfig.saveAll writes them as plaintext strings into the xiaoduo_net preferences file; BuildConfig constants embed build-time cloud keys into the APK DEX/resources. Sink: on-disk XML in the app sandbox and statically extractable constants in any distributed APK.
attackPath.reachability: Rooted device or brief local access reads the preferences XML directly; anyone holding a distributed APK extracts the built-in keys by static analysis; allowBackup=false blocks only the cloud-backup path.

confidence.rationale: Storage calls and BuildConfig wiring are direct, grep-verified facts; exposure follows from standard Android platform properties.

findings.remediation: Move secrets to Android Keystore-backed storage (e.g. EncryptedSharedPreferences or Jetpack Security) for password, token, and API keys; remove the BuildConfig-baked key fallback and require per-device key entry (or a backend-issued short-lived token); if a bundled key is unavoidable, scope it to a least-privilege proxy key.
remediationTests: Round-trip test: values written through NetConfig saveAll read back through the Keystore-backed store; grep-style contract test asserting no secret keys are written to plain SharedPreferences.
findings.rootCause: Secrets were treated as ordinary settings: the same SharedPreferences file that stores endpoint URLs also stores the password, bearer token, and vendor API keys, and a build-time convenience injects fallback keys as compile-time constants.
findings.summary: Account password, platform bearer token, and cloud API keys (OpenAI/Aliyun/Volcengine) are persisted in plaintext SharedPreferences, and BuildConfig-injected API keys are packaged into the APK where static extraction recovers them.
findings.title: Credentials and API keys stored in plaintext and packaged into the APK

validation.counterevidence: allowBackup=false and MODE_PRIVATE sandboxing reduce primary exposure to rooted devices; BUILTIN_* keys are blank unless the build injected secrets/cloud.properties, so packaged-key impact is conditional on the analyzed artifact — the unconditional plaintext storage path remains a real weakness.
validation.evidence: NetConfig.kt:236-263 writes KEY_PASSWORD/KEY_CLOUD_KEY/KEY_VOLC_SPEECH_KEY/KEY_ALIYUN_SPEECH_KEY as plaintext; TokenStore.kt:45 persists the token plaintext; NetConfig.kt:103-105 reads BuildConfig.CLOUD_KEY/ALIYUN_SPEECH_KEY/VOLC_SPEECH_KEY; repo-wide grep found no EncryptedSharedPreferences or Keystore usage.
validation.method: Repo-wide storage-path grep plus Android API surface check for Keystore/EncryptedSharedPreferences.

attackPath.dataflow: Source: uncaught exception stack traces (potentially containing endpoint URLs, file names, or user data in exception messages). Transform: CrashReporter.writeCrash appends them to files/logs/crash-<day>.log; LogRotator nameRegex only matches xiaoduo-<date>.log so neither PetLogger startup cleanup nor the export allowlist ever sees the crash files. Sink: unbounded accumulation of sensitive stack traces in the FileProvider-shared logs/ directory.
attackPath.reachability: Every crash appends a file that is never deleted for the lifetime of the app installation; on long-lived kiosk boards (the primary deployment target) this grows without bound and retains old crash content indefinitely.

confidence.rationale: The filename-prefix mismatch is mechanically verifiable across CrashReporter/LogRotator/PetLogger; no other cleanup path exists.

findings.remediation: Extend LogRotator (or add a sibling filter) to recognize crash-<date>.log and include those files in expiredFiles cleanup with their own retention window; alternatively have CrashReporter reuse the xiaoduo-<date>.log naming with a marker line, so a single filter governs rotation, cleanup, and export.
remediationTests: Unit test: expiredFiles([crash-2020-01-01.log], today) returns the stale crash file; integration test: simulated crash logs are deleted after KEEP_DAYS.
findings.rootCause: CrashReporter was added later with its own crash- prefix, but the retention policy stayed anchored to the xiaoduo-*.log name pattern, so the two filename conventions never reunited under one cleanup rule.
findings.summary: Crash logs are written as crash-YYYY-MM-DD.log but rotation, cleanup, and export filters only match xiaoduo-*.log, so stack traces accumulate indefinitely in the app logs directory (which is also the FileProvider root).
findings.title: Crash logs exempt from rotation and cleanup accumulate unbounded

validation.counterevidence: The files remain app-private and the share sheet filters them out, so the practical impact is unbounded growth and indefinite retention rather than direct disclosure; severity is low but the flaw is deterministic.
validation.evidence: CrashReporter.kt:17 PREFIX=crash- and :38 crashFileFor builds crash-<day>.log; LogRotator.kt:21 regex matches only xiaoduo-<date>.log; PetLogger.kt:29-33 cleanup and :41-47 logFiles() both filter through that regex; file_paths.xml exposes logs/ to FileProvider.
validation.method: Filename-convention mismatch traced across CrashReporter, LogRotator, PetLogger, and file_paths.xml.

attackPath.dataflow: Source: any co-installed app broadcasts com.xiaoduo.deskpet.DEBUG_BUBBLE[_APPEND|_HIDE] with a text extra. Transform: the receiver checks only ApplicationInfo.FLAG_DEBUGGABLE, then claims a DEBUG-owner bubble round and forwards the extra to PetOverlayService.showBubble. Sink: attacker-controlled text rendered in the SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW bubble above other apps (debug builds).
attackPath.reachability: On debug builds (the project's standard internal test artifacts) any app can trigger this with one broadcast and no permissions; release builds return before any action, so impact is confined to debuggable installations.

confidence.rationale: Code behavior is certain, but impact requires a debuggable build in the field plus a malicious co-installed app.

findings.remediation: Set android:exported="false" on the receiver for release builds (manifest placeholders or a debug-only manifest overlay), or add a signature-level custom permission to the intent filter; keep the adb (shell) path working by registering the receiver in debug-only source instead of the main manifest.
remediationTests: Robolectric test: broadcast from a non-debug application context is dropped; instrumented test: release build ignores DEBUG_BUBBLE actions.
findings.rootCause: ColorOS cannot deliver shell broadcasts to non-exported receivers, so the debug affordance was exported in the main manifest for all builds and the release safety was delegated entirely to a runtime FLAG_DEBUGGABLE check instead of manifest-level separation.
findings.summary: DebugBubbleReceiver is exported with no permission; in debug builds any co-installed app can drive the SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW bubble with arbitrary text, and release builds are protected only by the runtime FLAG_DEBUGGABLE guard.
findings.title: Exported debug bubble receiver guarded only by FLAG_DEBUGGABLE

validation.counterevidence: The guard fully protects release builds and the manifest documents the export as a deliberate ColorOS shell-broadcast affordance — accepted-risk counterevidence that narrows impact to debug distributions but does not close the debug-build attack path.
validation.evidence: AndroidManifest.xml:57-65 declares the receiver exported with three custom actions and no permission; DebugBubbleReceiver.kt:24 FLAG_DEBUGGABLE early-return is the only caller check; text flows to svc.showBubble(BubbleOwner.DEBUG, ...).
validation.method: Manifest export posture plus receiver guard and overlay sink trace.
